trial_name: AKIKI — Initiation Strategies for Renal-Replacement Therapy in the Intensive Care Unit (2016)
citation: Gaudry S, Hajage D, Schortgen F, Martin-Lefevre L, Pons B, Boulet E, et al. Initiation Strategies for Renal-Replacement Therapy in the Intensive Care Unit. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(2):122-133
one_liner: In severe ICU AKI without urgent indications, a delayed trigger-based RRT strategy resulted in similar 60-day mortality as immediate initiation while sparing nearly half of patients from RRT and reducing exposure-related complications.

pico.population: Adults (≥18) with KDIGO stage 3 AKI, requiring invasive mechanical ventilation and/or vasopressors, without immediate urgent RRT criteria (e.g., life-threatening hyperkalaemia, acidosis, pulmonary oedema)
pico.intervention: Immediate initiation of RRT as soon as possible after randomisation (target ≤6 h), modality at clinician discretion
pico.comparison: Delayed, trigger-based RRT: wait until any pre-specified criterion (potassium >6 mmol/L or >5.5 despite treatment, pH <7.15, urea >40 mmol/L, oliguria/anuria >72 h, severe pulmonary oedema with hypoxaemia); medical management of hyperkalaemia/acidosis and diuretics allowed

background.existing_knowledge: RRT is a high-frequency ICU intervention for severe AKI, but the optimal initiation timing in the absence of life-threatening complications was uncertain. Earlier initiation might prevent metabolic/volume complications and multi-organ failure, but exposes patients to catheter-related harms, haemodynamic instability, electrolyte derangements and resource use. Prior evidence was dominated by heterogeneous observational studies (strong confounding by indication) and small RCTs (e.g., ELAIN) which suggested possible benefit with early initiation.
background.knowledge_gap: No large pragmatic trial had defined a safe ‘watchful waiting’ strategy with explicit, reproducible triggers that could standardise the decision to start RRT.
background.hypothesis: A delayed, trigger-based initiation strategy would result in similar 60-day survival compared with immediate initiation, while reducing RRT exposure and associated complications.

methods.design: Prospective, multicentre, open-label, parallel-group randomised control trial with group-sequential design and two planned interim analyses.
methods.setting: 31 ICUs (medical and mixed) in France, enrolment September 2013 to January 2016.

inclusion: Adults ≥18 years with AKI compatible with acute tubular necrosis (ischaemic/toxic context) and KDIGO stage 3 (creatinine >354 µmol/L or ≥3× baseline; anuria >12 h; or oliguria <0.3 mL/kg/h for >24 h)
Plus invasive mechanical ventilation and/or continuous IV catecholamines
exclusion: Severe chronic kidney disease (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min)
Obstructive/vascular AKI, tumour lysis, thrombotic microangiopathy, acute glomerulopathy
Moribund state or decision to withhold/withdraw active treatment

Pre-randomisation urgent RRT indications: oliguria/anuria >3 days, serum potassium >6 mmol/L (or >5.5 despite medical therapy), serum urea >40 mmol/L, metabolic acidosis with pH <7.15, acute pulmonary oedema with severe hypoxaemia despite diuretics

methods.intervention: RRT initiated as soon as possible after randomisation (trial target ≤6 h). Modality (continuous or intermittent) chosen by treating team according to local practice and haemodynamic status.
methods.comparison: No RRT at randomisation. RRT initiated only if at least one pre-specified criterion occurred: hyperkalaemia (potassium >6 mmol/L or >5.5 despite medical treatment), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.15), acute pulmonary oedema due to fluid overload with severe hypoxaemia, serum urea >40 mmol/L, or oliguria/anuria persisting >72 h after randomisation. Co-interventions: medical management of hyperkalaemia/acidosis and diuretics permitted; RRT started promptly once criteria met. In the delayed group, the first qualifying criterion leading to RRT was: oliguria/anuria >72 h 36.3%, hyperkalaemia 26.8%, urea >40 mmol/L 18.5%, metabolic acidosis 15.3%, pulmonary oedema 2.6%. Median trigger-to-RRT latency was 4.7 h (IQR 3.0–7.8).
methods.blinding: Open-label; primary outcome (all-cause mortality) is objective, but co-interventions and decisions about RRT modality/dose could introduce performance bias.
methods.sample_size_power: 620 patients planned (powered to detect a 15 percentage-point absolute reduction in 60-day mortality from 55% to 40% with early initiation, two-sided α=0.05, 90% power, group-sequential design with 2 interim analyses inflated to 560, plus 10% anticipated loss to follow-up).
secondary_outcomes: Renal recovery at day 28 in survivors (RRT discontinued ≥7 days)
Dialysis dependence at day 60 in survivors

headline_bullets: 60-day mortality nearly identical: 48.5% early vs 49.7% delayed (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.82–1.29, P=0.79)
Delayed group avoided RRT entirely in 49% of patients (51% received RRT vs 98% early), with median time to first RRT 57 h vs 2 h
Early RRT increased catheter-related bloodstream infections (10% vs 5%, P=0.03) and hypophosphataemia (22% vs 15%, P=0.03)
No significant differences in renal recovery or dialysis dependence among survivors; haemorrhage rates similar (9% early vs 12% delayed, P=0.21)

outcomes_table.note: ITT analysis; denominators reflect available vital status (early 309/311, delayed 308/308) due to 1 withdrawal and few missing

Absolute reduction 47%; in delayed group, 151/308 (49%) never received RRT. Total RRT sessions: 1665 early vs 943 delayed; median sessions per treated patient: 3 (IQR 2–6) early vs 4 (IQR 2–8) delayed.

outcomes_table.outcome: Renal recovery at day 28 in survivors (RRT discontinued ≥7 days)
Dialysis dependence at day 60 in survivors

safety: Catheter-related bloodstream infection more frequent in early group (10% vs 5%, P=0.03)
Hypophosphataemia higher with early RRT (22% vs 15%, P=0.03)
Haemorrhage requiring transfusion not significantly different (9% early vs 12% delayed, P=0.21)
No other adverse safety signals associated with delayed strategy

domains.notes: Central web-based randomisation with stratification by centre and variable block sizes; allocation concealed until assignment. Eligibility confirmed and randomisation occurred shortly after meeting KDIGO stage 3 criteria (trial target ≤5 h), limiting immortal time bias.

Open-label design. Primary outcome (mortality) is objective. Trigger-based criteria in delayed arm reduced clinician discretion over ‘when’ to start RRT, improving protocol fidelity. However, co-interventions (diuretics, medical management of hyperkalaemia) differed substantially: diuretic use 1.3% early vs 36.5% delayed; medical treatment for hyperkalaemia 5.5% early vs 22.9% delayed, reflecting predictable protocol consequences.

Randomised 620 patients; 1 withdrew permission to use data (619 analysed). Vital status available: day 28 — early 308/311 (99%), delayed 306/308 (99.4%); day 60 — early 309/311 (99.4%), delayed 308/308 (100%). Primary analysis ITT.

Early arm: 6/311 (1.9%) did not receive RRT (3 ineligible inclusions who survived, 2 died before RRT, 1 assignment misread). Delayed arm: 5/308 (1.6%) received RRT without meeting criteria (misinterpretation of assignment/criteria). Excellent separation in RRT exposure (98% vs 51%).
Groups well matched: SOFA at randomisation 11±3 vs 11±3; SAPS III 73±12 vs 74±12; mechanical ventilation ~86–87%; vasopressors ~85–86%; sepsis ~80%.

domains.domain: Timing and dose of the intervention
domains.notes: Time to first RRT: median 2 h (IQR 1–3) early vs 57 h (IQR 25–83) delayed. Trigger-to-RRT latency in delayed arm: median 4.7 h (IQR 3.0–7.8). Biochemistry at RRT initiation (early vs delayed): creatinine 3.27 mg/dL (IQR 2.62–4.05) vs 5.33 (IQR 3.85–6.50); urea 52 mg/dL (IQR 40–65) vs 90 (IQR 65–106); potassium 4.4 mmol/L (IQR 3.8–4.8) vs 5.1 (IQR 4.4–5.7). RRT modality and prescription pragmatic, introducing within-group variability.

Primary outcome is objective mortality. Sequential design with planned interim analyses, group-sequential stopping rules, and intention-to-treat analysis supports inferential integrity. Trial powered for a large effect (15% absolute reduction); smaller mortality differences remain statistically uncertain.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall internal validity moderate to strong: robust randomisation and follow‑up with excellent separation in RRT exposure, but open‑label conduct and pragmatic co‑interventions introduce some performance‑bias risk (mitigated by objective mortality and protocolised delayed triggers).

domains.notes: Represents a common ICU phenotype: severe AKI with multi-organ failure (high rates of sepsis, mechanical ventilation, vasopressors). However, restricted to patients who have reached KDIGO stage 3 and require organ support; does not address earlier AKI (KDIGO 1–2), ward/non-ICU settings, or patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (eCrCl <30 mL/min), kidney transplant, Child–Pugh C cirrhosis, etc. who were excluded.

Delayed strategy requires close biochemical/clinical monitoring and capability to initiate RRT rapidly when triggers occur; centres with constrained access to RRT may not replicate the safety profile. Modality mix (intermittent vs continuous) and catheter-related complication rates may differ in other healthcare systems, influencing net benefit/harm.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate: findings apply well to adult, high-acuity ICU patients with KDIGO stage 3 AKI and ready access to RRT, but less clearly to earlier AKI, advanced chronic kidney disease, or resource-limited environments.

strengths: Large, multicentre pragmatic RCT with high follow-up completeness
Clinically meaningful primary endpoint (60-day mortality) and clear protocolised triggers for delayed RRT
Marked separation in RRT exposure (98% vs 51%) supports a valid test of the clinical strategy
limitations: Open-label conduct with potential co-intervention and behavioural effects (e.g., diuretics and medical rescue therapies differed markedly)
RRT modality and prescription were not standardised, increasing heterogeneity in delivered treatment
Powered for a large mortality effect (15% absolute); smaller but clinically relevant differences cannot be excluded
Restricted inclusion (KDIGO stage 3 plus organ support) limits inference for earlier AKI or less severely ill populations

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted pragmatic RCT demonstrating that protocolised delayed RRT initiation is safe and reduces unnecessary exposure in severe ICU AKI without urgent criteria; findings are robust for similar populations.
strengths: Large sample size with minimal attrition
Objective primary outcome and explicit trigger criteria enhance reproducibility
High protocol adherence and excellent group separation
weaknesses: Powered for large effect only, so smaller mortality differences remain uncertain
Limited generalisability to earlier AKI stages or resource-limited settings

sections.authors_conclusion: In ICU patients with KDIGO stage 3 AKI without urgent indications, a delayed strategy based on pre-specified triggers resulted in similar 60-day mortality as immediate initiation, while avoiding RRT in nearly half of patients.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Adopt an indications-based, rather than routine, RRT initiation strategy in severe ICU AKI: begin RRT only when specific biochemical or clinical triggers are met, not simply upon reaching KDIGO stage 3.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with KDIGO stage 3 AKI, mechanical ventilation or vasopressors, and no immediate life-threatening complications; with reliable monitoring and rapid RRT access.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That RRT can be indefinitely delayed or withheld in all patients; excessive delay (beyond the protocol’s criteria) may be harmful, as suggested by AKIKI2.
implementation_caveats: Close monitoring for the protocol triggers is essential
RRT must be available promptly once criteria are met
These findings may not extend to patients with advanced chronic kidney disease or those without organ support

controversies.notes: Differences in enrolment KDIGO stage and trigger sets between AKIKI and the single‑centre ELAIN trial complicate direct comparisons; AKIKI’s delayed triggers are similar to ELAIN’s ‘early’ arm, explaining apparently discordant findings.

IDEAL-ICU (septic shock, severe AKI) stopped early for futility, no mortality benefit to early initiation. STARRT-AKI (large international RCT) showed no reduction in 90‑day mortality with accelerated RRT while increasing adverse events. AKIKI2 suggested potential harm with a more‑delayed strategy, reinforcing a balanced ‘wait, but not too long’ paradigm.

An individual patient data meta‑analysis found no survival benefit to early initiation across RCTs, with increased RRT exposure in early strategies. A Cochrane review reached similar conclusions. ICU guidance increasingly supports starting RRT for conventional urgent indications and avoiding routine early initiation in their absence, aligning with AKIKI’s trigger‑based approach.

context_related_trials.relation: Single‑centre RCT that suggested mortality benefit with early initiation in KDIGO stage 2; its ‘early’ arm used triggers broadly similar to AKIKI’s delayed arm, so findings are not contradictory when accounting for patient selection and timing definitions.
Multicentre RCT in patients with septic shock and severe AKI; stopped early for futility, with no mortality benefit to early RRT, reinforcing AKIKI’s signal in a sepsis‑enriched population.
Largest international RCT to date; no reduction in 90‑day mortality with accelerated RRT, increased adverse events, strongly supporting an on‑demand rather than routine initiation strategy.

Follow‑up RCT testing a more‑delayed initiation strategy versus the standard delayed approach used in AKIKI; suggested potential harm with excessive delay, supporting a balanced ‘wait, but not too long’ paradigm.

unresolved_questions: Optimal timing in earlier AKI (KDIGO 1–2), patients with advanced CKD, and those not requiring organ support
Safety of more conservative triggers and impact on long‑term renal outcomes
Variation in effect by RRT modality and dose

numbers_to_remember: RRT avoided in 49% of delayed group
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: For severe ICU AKI without urgent indications, start RRT only when clear triggers arise, not routinely upon reaching stage 3, avoiding unnecessary dialysis and harm without impacting survival.
